content: Yang Luchan (1799–1872) survived the destruction of the Shaolin Temple during the Qing Dynasty. He was a significant figure in the development and teaching of Tai Chi Chuan, a soft-style martial art, in Beijing during the latter half of the 19th century. Yang is recognized as the founder of the Yang style of Tai Chi Chuan and played a pivotal role in transmitting the art to the Wu/Hao, Wu, and Sun Tai Chi families. The Ten Tigers of Canton, active in the late 1800s, were a group of ten highly skilled Chinese martial arts masters from Guangdong (Canton) during the late Qing Dynasty (1644–1912). Wong Kei-Ying, the father of Wong Fei Hung, was a member of this esteemed group. Wong Fei Hung (1847–1924) is celebrated as a Chinese folk hero during the Republican period. His life inspired over one hundred Hong Kong films, and his character has been portrayed by actors such as Sammo Hung, Jackie Chan, and Jet Li in blockbuster movies. Huo Yuanjia (1867–1910) was the founder of the Chin Woo Athletic Association and gained fame for his widely publicized matches against foreign fighters. His life story was depicted in the 2006 film Fearless. Yip Man (1893–1972) was a master of Wing Chun, a Southern Chinese martial art, and was the first to openly teach this style. He is best known as the teacher of Bruce Lee. Most of the major branches of Wing Chun that exist today were developed and promoted by Yip Man’s students. Bruce Lee (1940–1973) was a Chinese-American martial artist and actor who became an iconic figure of the 20th century. He practiced Wing Chun and popularized it globally. Using Wing Chun as his foundation, he later developed his own martial arts philosophy and methodology, which he named Jeet Kune Do. Jackie Chan (born 1954) is a Hong Kong martial artist and actor renowned for incorporating physical comedy into his martial arts performances and for executing complex stunts in his films. Jet Li (born 1963) is a five-time national Wushu champion in China who later showcased his martial arts skills in cinema, becoming a global star. Chinese martial arts have had a profound influence on popular culture. Historically, their impact can be seen in Asian literature and performance arts. In recent times, this influence has extended to movies and television, reaching a global audience. As a result, Chinese martial arts have transcended their ethnic origins and gained worldwide appeal. Martial arts play a central role in the literary genre known as wuxia (武侠小说), which revolves around themes of chivalry, a distinct martial arts society (Wulin, 武林), and martial arts as a core element. Wuxia stories date back to the 2nd and 3rd centuries BCE, gained popularity during the Tang Dynasty, and evolved into novel form by the Ming Dynasty. This genre remains highly popular across East Asia and significantly shapes public perceptions of martial arts. Chinese opera, particularly Beijing opera, also incorporates martial arts movements. This dramatic art form, which dates back to the Tang Dynasty, continues to be a vital expression of Chinese culture. Many martial artists have performed in Chinese operas, blending their skills with theatrical performance. In modern times, Chinese martial arts have given rise to the martial arts film genre. Bruce Lee’s films were instrumental in introducing Chinese martial arts to Western audiences in the 1970s. The American television series Kung Fu (1972–1975), with its 60 episodes, also played a significant role in popularizing Chinese martial arts and their philosophy in North America. Actors and martial artists like Jet Li and Jackie Chan have continued to captivate audiences with martial arts films. Chinese martial arts films, often referred to as Kung Fu movies (功夫片) or Wire Fu when extensive wirework is used for special effects, remain a hallmark of the Kung Fu theater tradition. While Chinese martial arts techniques are now commonly seen in television action series, the deeper philosophy behind these arts is rarely explored in depth.
